gs1-sunrise-2027-2d-barcode-transition.title: GS1 Sunrise 2027: The Transition to 2D Barcodes in Retail
gs1-sunrise-2027-2d-barcode-transition.excerpt: With GS1 Sunrise 2027, retail point-of-sale systems are expected to read 2D barcodes by the end of 2027. Learn about dual-marking, GS1 Digital Link, and production-line preparation steps.
gs1-sunrise-2027-2d-barcode-transition.content:
For more than fifty years, linear barcodes have automated product identification in the retail sector, but they have been limited to carrying only a single data element. GS1 Sunrise 2027 is a global industry initiative aimed at replacing this structure with two-dimensional (2D) barcodes capable of carrying significantly more information. According to the objective, also referred to as Ambition 2027, all retail point-of-sale systems are expected to be able to read and process GS1-compliant 2D barcodes alongside linear barcodes by the end of 2027.

Scope of the GS1 Sunrise 2027 Initiative

What Is GS1 Sunrise 2027?

GS1 Sunrise 2027 is not a deadline after which linear barcodes become invalid. Rather, it is a shared milestone established to ensure retail infrastructure is ready for 2D barcodes. The minimum objective is that a checkout scanner can capture the product identifier (GTIN) from both an EAN-13 barcode and a GS1-compliant 2D barcode and transmit it completely to the POS software. For example, even if a supermarket scanner can physically detect a QR code, the requirement is not fulfilled if it cannot interpret the embedded GS1 data.

The Data Limitations of Linear Barcodes

EAN-13 and UPC-A barcodes only carry the GTIN; they cannot include batch numbers, expiration dates, or serial numbers. GS1 DataBar Expanded partially addresses this limitation, but its capacity remains restricted and the symbol can become too large for smaller packages. For example, including weight, batch, and date information for fresh meat products in a single linear symbol may consume a substantial portion of the label area.

Accepted 2D Barcodes and Data Syntax

Only three options are accepted for point-of-sale use:

  • GS1 DataMatrix — encoded using GS1 element string syntax
  • QR Code — encoded using GS1 Digital Link URI syntax
  • Data Matrix — encoded using GS1 Digital Link URI syntax

The element string structure represents data through GS1 Application Identifiers (AIs); batch number (10), expiration date (17), and serial number (21) are encoded using this format. Digital Link carries the same information in a web-address format, connecting the barcode to digital content. For example, a QR code printed on a canned food label may transmit the GTIN at checkout while also directing consumers to a web page dedicated to that specific batch.

Packaging and Production During the Transition Period

The Dual-Marking Period and Placement Rules

During the transition period, products will carry both a linear barcode and a 2D barcode, a practice known as dual-marking. According to GS1 guidance, this approach remains necessary until at least 90% of point-of-sale scanners can extract the GTIN from GS1-compliant 2D barcodes. Extensive testing has shown that, to maintain a checkout speed of approximately 40 to 70 products per minute, the 2D barcode should be positioned no more than 50 mm from the center of the linear barcode. For example, a QR code placed too far away may require the cashier to rotate the product twice.

Dynamic Data Printing and Print Quality

Because the GTIN is static, the linear barcode is typically pre-printed by the packaging supplier. A 2D barcode, however, may contain variable data that changes from batch to batch and therefore must often be printed in real time on the production line. This requires continuous inkjet (CIJ), thermal transfer, or laser printing systems to receive accurate information from manufacturing management systems.

Readability depends on contrast and module size. The X-dimension of 2D barcodes is approximately 1.5 times larger than that of an equivalent linear barcode, and colors such as red, orange, and yellow may create scanning risks due to the characteristics of red-light scanners. For example, a QR code containing a logo may fail at checkout if the logo consumes too much error-correction capacity. Therefore, verification should be repeated under production conditions according to ISO/IEC 15415.

Traceability, Compliance, and Preparation

Traceability and Targeted Recalls

The most significant operational advantage of a 2D barcode is the ability to identify products at the batch or serial level. When the GTIN, batch number, and expiration date can all be scanned, a recall can be limited to the affected batch instead of the entire product range. The same data can also prevent expired products from being sold at checkout. For example, a food manufacturer can determine from a serial number which production shift and which raw material batch were involved in manufacturing a product that became the subject of a complaint.

Regulatory Compliance and the Digital Product Passport

The transition to 2D barcodes aligns with evolving European Union regulations regarding product information. The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation entered into force on 18 July 2024 and places the Digital Product Passport at the center of the framework, while product-specific obligations are being defined gradually through secondary legislation. Since access to the passport is expected to be provided through a data carrier, the 2D barcode on the packaging becomes a compliance tool. In the pharmaceutical sector, for example, GS1 DataMatrix has been used for years as a serial-number carrier, demonstrating the practicality of the model.

Preparation Steps and Future Outlook

An effective transition begins with a product data inventory. Every product should be verified to have a valid GTIN, after which the data elements to be included in the barcode should be selected and tested within ERP and MES systems. In Türkiye, company prefixes and GTIN allocations are managed through GS1 Türkiye.

For example, a pilot project involving a limited number of product codes can identify print-quality issues at production speeds before they affect the entire portfolio. Once widespread adoption is achieved, the focus will shift from the barcode itself to the underlying data layer, including resolver services and visibility data.

Conclusion

GS1 Sunrise 2027 is not a cut-off date ending fifty years of linear barcode dominance. Instead, it is a shared goal designed to prepare retail infrastructure for data-rich barcodes. During the transition period, products will carry both barcode types, while compliance with placement and print-quality requirements will protect checkout efficiency. For manufacturers, the primary challenges lie not in packaging design but in GTIN accuracy, dynamic data printing, and reliable data processing.

For facilities that can reliably generate batch and serial numbers during production, transitioning to 2D barcodes is largely a matter of transferring existing data onto the packaging. For this reason, preparation should begin not with barcode selection, but with the point where production data is collected.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is GS1 Sunrise 2027 mandatory for manufacturers?

The initiative is defined as a voluntary transition for brand owners. Obligations arise primarily from point-of-sale readiness targets and product-specific regulations. In practice, the main driver of adoption will be retail chains requiring suppliers to provide products with 2D barcodes.

Will our existing EAN-13 barcodes become invalid in 2027?

No. Linear barcodes will continue to coexist with 2D barcodes for as long as necessary. During the transition period, products carrying a 2D barcode should also include a linear barcode. Once widespread adoption has been achieved, brand owners may choose to use only a 2D barcode on their packaging.

How should companies choose between GS1 DataMatrix and QR Code?

The choice depends on the use case. GS1 DataMatrix occupies less space and is widely accepted in healthcare products. QR Codes encoded using GS1 Digital Link syntax can be read by standard smartphone cameras and therefore provide advantages for products that require consumer interaction.

the-importance-of-food-traceability-for-.title: The Importance of Food Traceability for End Consumers
the-importance-of-food-traceability-for-.excerpt: Food traceability plays a critical role in food safety, quality and consumer trust, as customers demand more transparency about the products they buy.
the-importance-of-food-traceability-for-.content:
Food traceability plays a critical role in ensuring food safety, quality and consumer satisfaction. Today end consumers increasingly demand clear information about the origin and processing of food products.

What Is Food Traceability?

Food traceability is the ability to follow a food product through all stages of production, processing and distribution. The FAO defines food traceability as "the recording and monitoring of food products throughout production, processing and distribution" (FAO, 2015). This process allows consumers to learn where their food comes from and how it was processed.

Why Food Traceability Matters for Consumers

  • Food Safety: Traceability systems enable rapid identification and removal of risks, facilitating effective recalls. The lack of traceability in the 2006 E. coli outbreak damaged many brand reputations (FDA, 2007).
  • Transparency and Trust: Research shows that companies offering transparent brands increase consumer confidence. According to Nielsen's 2015 report, 66% of consumers seek sustainability and ethical production information (Nielsen, 2015).
  • Quality Perception: Traceability enables continuous monitoring of product quality. The Mintel 2020 report reveals that 60% of consumers are willing to pay more for high-quality products (Mintel, 2020).
  • Social Responsibility: Consumers prefer brands with environmental and social responsibility. Research shows 73% of consumers tend to buy sustainable products (McKinsey, 2020).
  • Differentiation: In a competitive market, traceability provides a differentiation advantage, helping brands stand out.

Forecasts for the Next Five Years

  • Digitalisation: Technologies like blockchain will further advance food traceability systems, allowing consumers to easily verify product histories.
  • Rising Consumer Demands: Growing consumer interest in health, safety and the environment will make effective traceability systems essential.
  • Regulation: Stricter regulations will push companies to standardise their systems and boost consumer confidence.
  • Sustainability Focus: Demand for sustainable agriculture and food production will increase, encouraging traceability systems to develop in this direction.

product-traceability-why-is-it-essential.title: Product Traceability: Why Is It Essential for Quality, Trust and Sustainability?
product-traceability-why-is-it-essential.excerpt: Product traceability is a strategic imperative linking quality assurance, regulatory compliance and sustainable supply-chain practices.
product-traceability-why-is-it-essential.content:
Product traceability has become a strategic requirement for modern businesses, linking quality assurance, customer trust and sustainable supply-chain practices together.

Product Traceability and Quality

Traceability systems support continuous quality monitoring throughout the production process. When errors or deviations are detected, defective products can be prevented from reaching the market, reducing costly recalls and rework.

Product Traceability and Trust

Consumers and business partners increasingly expect transparency. Providing detailed product history builds long-term trust and brand loyalty. Businesses that can demonstrate the origin, handling and compliance of every product gain a clear competitive advantage.

Product Traceability and Sustainability

Traceability enables companies to monitor environmental impact across the supply chain, from raw materials to delivery. This data is essential for sustainability reporting and for meeting growing regulatory and customer expectations around ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) standards.

Legal Compliance

Many industries are subject to strict traceability regulations. Maintaining comprehensive traceability records protects businesses in the event of audits, disputes or product recalls.

food-traceability-and-standards-the-impo.title: Food Traceability and Standards: Product, Carton and Pallet Traceability
food-traceability-and-standards-the-impo.excerpt: Product, carton and pallet traceability strengthens food safety, compliance and supply-chain transparency from production to consumption.
food-traceability-and-standards-the-impo.content:
In the food industry, traceability refers to the tracking and documentation of all processes from production to consumption. This process plays a critical role in ensuring food safety and quality control.

Core Elements of Food Traceability

Food Safety: Traceability systems track every stage of a food product's journey from production to the end consumer, enabling rapid and effective recalls in case of quality issues.

Legal Compliance: Many countries have implemented strict regulations regarding food traceability. Traceability systems facilitate adherence to these legal obligations.

Quality Control: Traceability enables continuous monitoring of products' compliance with quality standards. Defective products can be prevented from reaching the market when errors are detected during production.

Importance of Product, Carton and Pallet Traceability

Detailed Tracking: Tracking which products are placed in which cartons and which cartons are loaded onto which pallets allows for faster and more targeted interventions when issues are detected.

Efficiency: Carton and pallet-level traceability makes logistics processes more efficient, reducing errors during storage, transportation and distribution.

Transparency: Providing transparency throughout the supply chain builds trust for both producers and consumers.

Risk Management: In the event of contamination or quality issues, the source can be quickly identified and affected products recalled.

Food Traceability Standards

ISO 22000: A food safety management system standard based on HACCP principles. HACCP: Identifies and controls food safety risks at every stage of the production process. BRC Global Standards: Criteria for food safety, quality and operations. IFS: Quality and safety standards for food production processes. GlobalG.A.P.: A standard for good agricultural practices at the farm level.

barcode-systems-used-in-traceability.title: Barcode Systems Used in Traceability
barcode-systems-used-in-traceability.excerpt: Barcode systems are indispensable for traceability, process efficiency and product visibility across global supply chains.
barcode-systems-used-in-traceability.content:
In today's rapidly digitalising world, barcode systems have become indispensable for enhancing efficiency in production and logistics processes, ensuring product traceability, and streamlining operations.

The history of barcode technology began in 1948 with the development of the first optical scanning system by Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver. The first barcode scanner was used in a U.S. supermarket in 1974, marking the beginning of widespread commercial adoption. In Turkey, barcode technology was first implemented in 1988.

Commonly Used Barcode Systems

  • EAN-8 / EAN-13: Small and retail products — globally used for product identification.
  • UPC-A / UPC-E: Widely used in the United States for retail product identification.
  • Code 39 / Code 128: Industrial applications, logistics — support alphanumeric characters with variable-length data.
  • QR Code: Mobile payments, product information — high data capacity, fast reading.
  • Data Matrix: Electronic components, pharmaceuticals — stores large amounts of data in small spaces.
  • PDF417: Identification cards, travel documents — capable of encoding large datasets.
  • ITF (Interleaved 2 of 5): Carton boxes and logistics — high reading speed and accuracy.
  • GS1-128: Logistics, transportation, warehousing — high data capacity with application identifiers.
  • Aztec Code: Travel documents, mobile ticketing — fast reading with robust error correction.
  • MaxiCode: Package tracking — primarily used by UPS for fast logistics scanning.
  • GS1 DataBar Expanded: Fresh produce, variable-weight products — encodes serial numbers, lot numbers and expiry dates.
  • Pharmacode: Pharmaceutical industry — used for error detection in drug packaging.

The barcode technologies we extensively use in our traceability solutions are critical for ensuring products are traceable at every step from production to consumption.

how-to-implement-individual-product-trac.title: How to Implement Individual Product Traceability
how-to-implement-individual-product-trac.excerpt: A practical framework for implementing individual product traceability with unique coding, marking strategy and process-wide verification.
how-to-implement-individual-product-trac.content:
"I want to track products individually." A simple sentence — but when you add "How can I do this?", the process becomes far more complex. Tracking individual products requires careful consideration, planning and integration of multiple components.

The first essential rule of individual product traceability is assigning a unique code to each product. The initial analysis should focus on how the product will be marked and which technology will be used.

Question 1: Is the product's structure suitable for marking? Where should marking be applied?

Examine the product and collaborate with departments such as marketing, sales, quality, R&D and production to make a consolidated decision.

Question 2: Which operations require marking beforehand?

Think of traceability processes as a chain. You can start with a small traceability system and add new links as needed.

Question 3: Can the code on the product be carried through all operations?

While the product may allow marking at the first station, subsequent operations like ovens, painting or sanding may affect code readability. You must ensure the code remains readable throughout the production process.

Question 4: Which marking technology should be used?

Various technologies can be used: inkjet, thermal transfer, laser/carbon fibre printers, or RFID tags. Based on the analysis, you may need heat-resistant labels or high-powered laser printers. A holistic evaluation of cycle times, process flow, machine locations and space constraints is essential.

The second critical step is ensuring codes are scanned before each operation.

what-are-the-benefits-of-traceability-sy.title: What Are the Benefits of Traceability Systems?
what-are-the-benefits-of-traceability-sy.excerpt: As quality expectations rise, traceability systems help reduce rework, improve cost control and support continuous improvement.
what-are-the-benefits-of-traceability-sy.content:
With the advancement of technology, the rules of the game in the manufacturing sector are changing. Many companies now use similar machine technologies. So what sets companies apart today? The answer is quality.

Producing more in the same amount of time is no longer enough; high-quality production with low rework rates is increasingly critical. As a result, the need for traceability systems is growing day by day.

Benefits of Traceability Systems

Improved Production Quality

Traceability systems incorporate quality control points into the production process, helping to prevent critical errors and enhance overall production quality.

Reduced Rework Rates and Production Costs

By detecting production errors early through process controls, issues are resolved quickly. This reduces rework labour and lowers production costs.

Supports Root Cause Analysis

Traceability systems provide access to data from every stage of the production process, enabling identification and resolution of the root causes of issues.

Clarifies Inter-Operation Cost Analysis

By tracking the flow of the production process, traceability systems allow clear observation of cost and value streams within the process.

Facilitates Continuous Improvement

Monitoring how parts and products move between lines makes continuous improvement easier. Knowing where and when bottlenecks or delays occur enables real-time optimisation.

In addition to these benefits, regulations in some industries mandate traceability systems. Sectors like healthcare and pharmaceuticals lead the way, and new regulations indicate many other industries will follow.

what-are-traceability-data-definition-of.title: What Are Traceability Data? Definition of Traceability
what-are-traceability-data-definition-of.excerpt: Traceability data captures production, quality and process events at serial level to support reliable quality management and compliance.
what-are-traceability-data-definition-of.content:
Traceability data is, at its core, quite simple. Traceability involves recording all events that affect a product. This data is collected throughout the entire production process — including materials added (BOM and critical components), tools used, process steps performed and test results — all recorded based on serial numbers.

It is common to see traceability data collected manually. Any data collection involving human intervention raises concerns about reliability. Manually collected paper data is highly prone to errors. Additionally, assigning operators extra data-recording responsibilities creates hidden costs for businesses.

Values of Traceability: Active Quality Management

Rather than focusing solely on traceability data for product recall scenarios, it is far more valuable to view traceability data as a real-time quality management tool. With reliable and detailed traceability data, a root cause analysis can be conducted to identify the conditions and events leading to a defect. As part of a Quality Management System, corrective actions can be defined and implemented to ensure the error never recurs. Digital traceability enables businesses to achieve real and continuous improvement toward zero-defect production.

Values of Traceability: Compliance

As electronics have become critical in industries such as automotive, white goods and aerospace, the reliability of electronic products is paramount. Compliance with agreed-upon rules and procedures protects suppliers by proving that no errors occurred in the production of a defective product. Traceability data meets these requirements instantly, safeguarding suppliers from costly legal disputes.

bomi-group-camera-based-multi-code-readi.title: BOMI Group Camera-Based Multi-Code Reading System
bomi-group-camera-based-multi-code-readi.excerpt: A camera-based multi-code reading implementation for BOMI that improved verification speed and reduced manual errors in warehouse operations.
bomi-group-camera-based-multi-code-readi.content:
For the Turkey warehouse of BOMI Group, a global leader in pharmaceutical logistics, we developed a Camera-Based Multi-Code Reading System, automating processes previously performed manually.

The line, tailored to BOMI's needs, consists of a 3-metre conveyor, 6 SICK cameras, an operator screen and a handheld terminal.

This system enables automatic verification of products on the order list, speeding up the process and eliminating human errors. An operator places a box containing 50 products on the conveyor. The box enters an enclosed area where cameras begin capturing images. Within seconds, Data Matrix codes are read and displayed on the system and operator screen. The codes are compared with the order list to ensure compliance with BOMI standards. Non-compliant codes are highlighted in red, prompting error correction and re-scanning. Once approved by the operator, the order is finalised.

If needed, products can be added manually using the handheld terminal.

With our Camera-Based Multi-Code Reading System, SISKON has supported BOMI in achieving significant advancements in warehouse management. This system, adaptable to various industries and applications, can add value to your business processes.

tusiad-sd2-pioneering-digital-transforma.title: TÜSİAD SD2: Pioneering Digital Transformation in Industry
tusiad-sd2-pioneering-digital-transforma.excerpt: Highlights from TÜSİAD SD2, where technology users and suppliers collaborated to accelerate industrial digital transformation.
tusiad-sd2-pioneering-digital-transforma.content:
As the first comprehensive program focused on digital transformation in industry, TÜSİAD SD2 brought together 18 leading technology user companies with SME-scale technology suppliers.

The second year of TÜSİAD's SD2 program is underway. Sponsored by Vodafone Business and Inventram and supported legally by Gün+Partners, the program connects technology user companies seeking digital transformation with the right solution partners while providing technology suppliers a platform to showcase and validate their solutions.

On Tuesday, 10 September, 18 technology user companies and shortlisted micro, small and medium-sized technology suppliers came together at the Industry-Technology Integration Program (STEP). During the STEP event, matches were made between technology users and pre-selected technology suppliers. The resulting success stories will be shared at the Digital Transformation Success Stories Ceremony at year-end.

The opening speech was delivered by TÜSİAD Vice President Bahadır Balkır, who highlighted the increasing uncertainties decision-makers face with the Fourth Industrial Revolution. TÜSİAD Board President Simone Kaslowski emphasised the intense competitive environment driven by digital transformation.

STEP Event Key Figures

  • Technology User Companies: 18
  • Technology Suppliers Submitting Solutions: 274
  • Shortlisted Suppliers Invited to STEP: 100
  • STEP Event Participants: 329

Notable match: Kordsa was matched with SISKON, marking our participation in this important digital transformation initiative.

chestny-znak-procedure-russias-digital-t.title: Chestny ZNAK Procedure: Russia's Digital Traceability System
chestny-znak-procedure-russias-digital-t.excerpt: Launched in 2019, Chestny ZNAK is a mandatory digital traceability platform that allows goods to be tracked through unique identifiers throughout the entire supply chain.
chestny-znak-procedure-russias-digital-t.content:
To combat counterfeiting and increase consumer trust in global supply chains, various traceability systems have been developed. The Chestny ZNAK system, implemented in the Russian Federation, is one of the most comprehensive systems designed for this purpose. Launched in 2019, Chestny ZNAK is a mandatory digital traceability platform that allows goods to be tracked through unique identifiers throughout the entire supply chain.

What is the Chestny ZNAK System?

Developed by the Russian government, Chestny ZNAK translates to "honest label" and is a traceability system designed to prevent counterfeiting and illegal trade by uniquely identifying each product. The system mandates the labeling of all products with either a QR code or a Data Matrix code. These codes enable products to be tracked throughout the entire supply chain. Each code is registered in the Chestny ZNAK database and can be verified by authorities and consumers.

Sectors Covered by Chestny ZNAK

Initially mandatory for specific product categories, the Chestny ZNAK system has been expanded to include the following main sectors:

  • Tobacco and cigarettes
  • Pharmaceuticals and medical products
  • Footwear and leather goods
  • Perfumes and cosmetics
  • Consumer electronics and home appliances
  • Automotive tires and parts
  • Apparel and textiles
  • Dairy and milk products
  • Alcohol and alcoholic beverages

How Does the Chestny ZNAK System Work?

The Chestny ZNAK procedure primarily consists of the following steps:

Registration and Authorization

  • Companies must register in the Chestny ZNAK system.
  • Necessary authorization processes are completed to register products.
Generation of Codes
  • A unique Data Matrix code is generated in the Chestny ZNAK database for each product.
  • These codes are printed on the product packaging.
Tracking the Supply Chain
  • Products are tracked at every stage by scanning the codes.
  • Wholesalers, retailers, and logistics companies record and track product movements in the Chestny ZNAK system.
Verification by Consumers
  • End consumers can scan the QR code with their mobile phones to verify the authenticity of the product.
Audit and Reporting
  • Regulatory authorities can use the data in the system to detect counterfeit products.

Onsuite Trace architecture seamlessly integrates with these regulations by fully digitizing traceability in compliance with Chestny ZNAK standards.
